video_title: Roman Mars on Flags, Phones, and the Design of Everyday Life
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,   I am speaking with design expert Roman Mars. He is  the host and creator of the podcast 99% Invisible,   which he describes as a sound-rich narrative  podcast, and it’s about the unnoticed   architectural and design choices that shape our  world. It is one of the most listened-to podcasts,   and it now has over 500 million downloads. He also  has an excellent book, The 99% Invisible City:   A Field Guide to the Hidden World of Everyday  Design, also with Kurt Kohlstedt. Roman, welcome. ROMAN MARS: Oh, thank you so much for  having me. It’s a pleasure to be here. COWEN: I have many design  questions for you. Let’s start. MARS: I hope I have design answers for you. COWEN: This, I think, is a hard one because  I found it hard, but where do you think   in the world the street signs are the most  attractive, and what makes them that way? MARS: Oh, my Lord. I don’t know if I know a  good answer for this. I’d be happy to hear   your answer. What I find, mostly as I’m getting  older, is that the most beautiful street signs are   the ones I can see the best. I’m always confounded  by the fact that, especially as a pedestrian,   street signs are often, the vantage point that  they’re really concerned about is a driver versus   a walker. As a walker, you’ll find that the  street sign is placed before the intersection,   that it’s for the driver approaching. You’ll be  on a corner and you’ll be looking around New York,   and you’re like, “I don’t know where I  am,” because it’s a little bit behind you. Yes, I don’t know if I have a favorite, like  really beautiful one in particular, but I do love   a really good grid. I like a street that  you know how to navigate without too   much looking at your phone. That makes me  very happy. I also love to get lost in the   alleys of Venice too. You just have to forge  ahead, and you’ll get there eventually. COWEN: Venice has good street signs, but  for size, I would go with Los Angeles. MARS: Yes, they’re quite big. COWEN: They’re designed for drivers.   I think for quality, most people would say some  mix of Spain and Portugal, which have these   ceramic themes. They’re not my favorites,  but they would be classic choices. MARS: I’ve only been to Spain a little  bit. Yes, they’re really quite beautiful.   There’s an abundance of good choices,  but to me, it’s about functionality. COWEN: I like the more artistic Switzerland, where  there’s just the name and a color, and there’s   blue and green, and it tells you how big a street  or highway it will be, and everything is stark and   it’s in this very Swiss font. That’s my personal  favorite, but I don’t think it would win a poll. MARS: It just matters if it works for you. COWEN: Yes. Here’s another question I’ve  thought about: Why is it that older cars,   maybe most classically from the early 1960s,  but not only, they’re so much more attractive   than today. Today, so many cars are SUVs, they  look literally the same. They’re so boring.   They’re not offensive, but in the aggregate,  maybe they’re offensive. What happened? MARS: This is confounding to me. I’ve talked to  a lot of industrial designers and designers over   the years, and cars are often the way they got  into design, caring about design as kids. That’s   the first thing they ever noticed and really loved  and cared about. A lot of it has to do with those   forms that were so bold; it was a  game on the highway where you could   look ahead of you and from just the shape, you  could say what model and make of car, maybe   what year of car. It was so distinctive. Now,  I think you couldn’t do that at all as a game. I think that there’s boring and plain reasons for  this, which are just energy resources and things.   We put a lot of steel unnecessarily in cars during  our extractive phase of manufacturing, where we   made big and bold choices because we didn’t care  that the things got 10 miles to the gallon and   the shapes of the fins and the structures were  ridiculously unsafe for the people inside.   Those get shaved down by necessity and the  needs of the environment, the needs of society. Then I think that there’s something about  people gravitating toward a mean and trying   to mass-produce something that appeals to  the biggest number of people, and then it   gets increasingly more and more  same-y. I do think it’s a real shame.   The moments where there are all these breakout  moments of something looking really different,   I have to admit, I don’t really like  them necessarily when they do. I think   the Cybertruck is a horrible-looking  vehicle, but it looks a lot different,   mainly because its utility is quite terrible.  Yes, it’s a real risk to go far afield and try   to create something brand new. I think there’s  a few pressures working to make things the same. COWEN: Do you find Waymos attractive? Because I  do. They look different. They look futuristic. MARS: Because of all the gadgetry on top? COWEN: The whirring thing on top. It’s almost  satire how they look, but I enjoy it. I smile. MARS: I’ve never been in a Waymo. This is my own  personal thing: This is getting very personal   very fast, but my one recurring nightmare  when I’m very, very stressed is I’m in the   backseat of a car with nobody driving, and I’m  trying to climb over to control the vehicle.   They’re not made for me in that sense because I  feel like if I was choosing to make that choice.   But Waymos seem very great. I think studies  are very clear that a robot-driving car is   way better than a human-driving car, so  I have no problem personally with them. COWEN: Do you think the nightmare  goes away if you confront it? MARS: Maybe. I think there’s a chance of that. It  is my one recurring thing is being in a speeding,   uncontrolled car, and I have to climb  over from the backseat to control it. COWEN: Now, I grew up in New Jersey, where we  have what’s sometimes called the panhandle. MARS: Jughandles. COWEN: Jughandles, as a way of making left turns.  You go around and then through from the side.   Do you feel we underuse those, or  should even New Jersey not have them? MARS: There’s some good thought and efficiency  built into jughandles. The problem is they really   only work if you know they’re coming.  If you’re familiar with the streets,   it is a nice thing of avoiding long left  turns or people waiting to make left turns.   If you don’t know the street, like  I’ve driven around in Jersey a lot,   and it’s just you don’t know if you  should be on the left or the right. I’m a driver who likes to be in the lane I’m  in very, very early. Making a rapid decision   realizing that, all of a sudden, that you’re  going to have to make a right to make a left is   something that also just really stresses me out.  If it was consistently used and there were never   lefts, I’d be all for it. It’s the inconsistency  which I think is a little bit of a problem. COWEN: Maybe no one really  visits New Jersey, right?   You wouldn’t do it in California or  Florida where plenty of people visit. MARS: Yes, that’s true. It is definitely  made for the people who are there. COWEN: People in New Jersey, they don’t even  visit other parts of New Jersey unless it’s   what they call the New Jersey Shore. Only in  New Jersey do they call it the shore, right? MARS: Fair enough. COWEN: Not beach, it’s the shore. MARS: That’s right. COWEN: Thus it may work there. I worry  that as the value of land goes up,   the jughandle or panhandle, it takes up more land. MARS: It certainly does. UPS has algorithms  where they make sure their drivers never make a   left turn because it is just so inefficient and so  bad for their routes. I’m of that belief. I’ll go   way around the block to make sure I’m not making  a left in a place that I’m not confident making   a left. I think the jughandle does serve a real  good purpose. It’s just the amount that has to be   telegraphed to a person not familiar with them  means that its utility is somewhat diminished. COWEN: What do you think of yellow  lighting on our roads? When I was a kid,   that was a trend for a while. I never  saw it take off. Is there any advantage? MARS: Yellow lighting, like as  in the overhead streetlights? COWEN: Instead of white. MARS: I don’t really know what the advantage is. I  haven’t really thought about it too much. I think   getting things toward more natural light and less  glaring light is important in terms of our sense   of the world and how much we want to engage with  the night sky and stuff like that. As long as it’s   thoughtful in terms of light pollution, mostly  it’s a good thing, but I’m not quite sure in   this case. I did interview a group of designers  who had a company called Civil Twilight, and it   was all about making streetlights a little bit  more responsive, a little less glaring, allowing   us to have a little bit more vision of the night  sky in our cities. I’m all for that type of thing. COWEN: What color should the central stripe be? MARS: On a road? COWEN: On a road, yes. Just white? MARS: I think the utility makes sense.  It’s white on the outside, it’s yellow   on the inside if you don’t want it to cross,  like double line if you don’t want to cross.   I think that’s pretty good. I like  the cat’s eyes reflective little   markers that I think help me out a lot, again,  as my vision is not as good as it used to be.   I really rely on these retroreflective  paints and cat’s eye, different things   to make it so that I can see them. That’s the  most important thing is being able to see them. COWEN: Now, if I think of small towns in New  England, many are quite charming or beautiful.   If I think of Houston, not that much of  it is attractive to me. Yet, Houston is   growing pretty rapidly and the small towns are  shrinking. How should I interpret that trend? MARS: Houston is a place famously with no zoning  laws whatsoever. That does create a type of growth   that is valuable to some. I think it has its  limits. What it does is it creates car culture,   which is, I think, a net negative  to only build a city around a car. COWEN: If it’s a net negative,  why is everyone moving there? Or   like northern Florida, which is also car  culture, growing rapidly in population? MARS: Definitely when you  ease those burdens of growth,   growth is easier. I think that’s pretty clear.  Then when growth is easier, cost is down.   It’s all about making choices. I think  that there’s going to be a group of people   that find that to be perfectly great and  perfectly that’s the world that they want,   and there’s enough populace in the United States  and a heterogeneity of what they care about that   that’ll be attractive, and then there’ll be places  where that’s not attractive. There’s definitely   enough population to support it regardless, and so  it’s fine that they have a place to go, for sure. COWEN: Can you see a world coming, just say in the  United States, where actually where people live   becomes more attractive on average and we build  new things, maybe in different styles, but they’re   attractive as small New England towns might be  attractive, and the country overall, the living   structures become more beautiful? Is there a  path toward that, or is that just impossible now? MARS: No, it’s not impossible. I do think  these things change and our sense of them   of what is attractive and what isn’t will  modify us over time. I do think there’s real   care and design in new structures. I’ve definitely  seen them in places that I’ve visited. I   was in New York recently. I think the best example  of this is London, which has a lot of historic   buildings, and the integration with the new modern  buildings, often inside of the same building, is   gorgeous. Really, really well done. There’s a  way to do it so that there’s a harmony amongst   these things. I think it has to do with the  trends in cities and what they’re going for. There’s a habit of care that is  retained. When you go to Chicago   and you see all the skyscrapers, there was an  onus on each of the different architectural firms   to have the skyscrapers talk to each other, even  across decades. I think it was a cultural thing,   not just about money or economics or something  like that. I think there was just a sense that the   Trump International Hotel, it had these different  levels, and one of those levels is the exact same   height as the Wrigley Building, and the next  level is the height of the next building around. It has these things that speak to  the area, that speak to beauty.   I think there’s something about them  that there’s a culture of that can   be retained and brought forward. I think  it’s present. I think there’s definitely   ways to make things beautiful and  continue to make things beautiful. COWEN: Would you say, is there any residential  neighborhood, take just the United States,   post-World War II, that you would say is beautiful  in the same way you would say Shaker Heights   is beautiful or some suburbs of Chicago are  beautiful? Because I can’t think of one, frankly. MARS: I can’t think of a beautiful suburb. COWEN: Now, I would say parts of Copenhagen  are quite new and beautiful, parts of Helsinki,   but there’s not much in the Western world.  In the US, I can’t think of anything. MARS: I don’t know if I can think of  something off the top of my head like that. COWEN: You’re a design expert. I’m not  criticizing you. I’m agreeing with you.   What has gone wrong with us?  What’s your account of this? MARS: I think it’s just about what  people want. I think a little bit of   the cohesion and harmony of a place   has to do with proximity and putting things close  together and people noticing. When you have places   that are further apart, like buildings, even  just houses that are further apart, and you have   the pressures of industrial manufacturing—housing  is one of those things that economists and people   thinking about it have always tried to  make it cheaper and cheaper and cheaper,   and in a way, it has a speed of light that they  can’t quite crack because building is local. They try to make things more modular.  They try to make it more cookie cutter.   At a certain point, they just can’t break through  a certain level. I was talking to Stephen Dubner   from Freakonomics about this at one point.  We were discussing this idea. I was like,   “I don’t want building to get more efficient.  I want it to be inefficient in ways because I   want people to make individual decisions and I  want local workers to be paid a certain amount   of money.” I think there’s an impulse to push  things to be more uniform and, I think, in a way,   less beautiful, but there’ll always be those  pockets where beauty and good design can be found. I think these things shift back and  forth in terms of what people care about   and just a matter of finding the right  collection of people that are willing to   put up with it at a level of  inefficiency to pay for the beauty. COWEN: Why wasn’t the Chrysler  Building more popular at first? MARS: It landed at a time period of the upswing of  modernism. It has all these, what are considered   at the time to be garish adornments, like the  silver hubcaps and the eagles and things to evoke   cars like the Chrysler. Modernists, especially  architecture critics at the time, were like,   “Oh, this is silly filigree on this building.”  I think it’s gorgeous. I love that building. COWEN: Same here. MARS: Its harsh criticism  and was a victim of the era.   Since then, I think it’s endured, and that’s why  it’s great to have buildings around for a while to   have them reassessed. Most of the buildings  that I’ve ever done stories about have been   reassessed over and over and over again.  You just have to be there long enough. COWEN: Do you enjoy brutalism? MARS: I do. Again, it’s something that it can  be done right or it can be done wrong. I think   one of the things about brutalism, why it appeals  to invested architecture fans and architects is,   in the abstract, the shapes and the forms are  really beautiful, especially as a drawing.   I think what brutalism fails is that it  doesn’t age particularly well because the   way the concrete aggregate, it can fall apart,  it can get cracked, it can feel heavy and   just intense. There’s places where  that brutalism form makes things   just oppressive and feel inhuman, and there’s  places where it feels extremely human and lovely. I love the Barbican in London. I think there’s a   functionality to that place that’s really  gorgeous, and the shapes of it are gorgeous.   You can do it well and then you can do  it in ways that are shocking to people. COWEN: Which do you think are cities that  do a good job incorporating greenery? MARS: I think that all of them   have gone through phases where they really  cared and where they haven’t. One of the   things I think about when it comes to New  York City in particular, I just think that   everyone should take a minute, all the time,  to recognize the miracle of Central Park.   The most expensive real estate in the world,  probably, for much of its time in existence   was held off to create this space  for people and that that place was   revolutionized through Olmsted; revolutionized  in the sense of what we treat parks and how   they speak to nature in a real way. That’s  just a stunning achievement to me. I think   of that. I live in the Bay Area. Golden Gate Park,  similarly, the existence of it is stunning to me. COWEN: Would Paris be better if  it had such a park? Because you’d   be pushing out a lot of Parisians. MARS: Yes. Probably. When you make  those decisions long ago, it’s easier to   value those decisions. If you were to raze a  whole neighborhood to the ground, several blocks,   it would be a harder ROI to calculate. I do think  that green spaces and public gathering spaces are   extremely important to a city, and when they  don’t have them, they suffer greatly for them. COWEN: What did Jane Jacobs get wrong? MARS: There’s a dichotomy that people draw  of the Jane Jacobs versus the Robert Moses   style of bottom-up versus top-down.  I do think that Jane Jacobs’ sense   of what a city or neighborhood should and could be  coming from the ground up is extremely astute and   on the money. I think her sense of the sidewalk  ballet and all those things are really important,   and they’re keen observations. I do think  that, taken to an extreme, there is a sense   that there is no good from top-down  planning, and I actually think that there is. I think that a functioning city operates both  top-down and bottom-up, and they both listen to   each other and they make big plans. There’s  not a lot of room in the Jacobs’ worldview,   in the extreme, for top-down plans that  really do matter and are effective and   make the world a better place. There can be  a historic preservationist streak in that,   a NIMBYism inside of Jane Jacobs that  I think could have a pernicious effect.   It isn’t present in her writing, but I think that  the natural follow-through has that potential. COWEN: What would she have thought of e-bike  lanes, which we now have a lot of in many places? MARS: I don’t know. Do they contribute to  the sidewalk ballet? I’m going to guess.   I’m going to say a little bit no and a little  bit yes. I don’t know how she would land on   e-bikes. I don’t know. It’s a good question. COWEN: What’s your view? Do they make cities  uglier or more attractive? I would say uglier. MARS: The e-bike lanes in  particular or just the e-bikes? COWEN: Both, if you have the lanes. MARS: I think that streets do need to be reclaimed  as a place of multimodal transportation, not just   given over to cars. I think that’s a good impulse.  The street existed in human history as a place for   humans, and horses, and carts, and eventually  cars, and then a change came and then they were   just only for cars and you were at fault if you  were a human inside of that street if anything   went wrong. I think that making streets more  flexible, more multimodal is a good impulse. I think the bikes are fine, I think the lanes are  fine as long as they work well. I think they’re   important toward deconstructing the hegemony of a  car. I think a car is a good thing. I have a car.   I like it. It’s good in some environments.  It’s not ideal for cities in a lot of ways.   It’s important to have different ways  to break apart the mobility of a city. COWEN: The land costs a lot. What do you  think of the Tokyo and Japanese model   where there’s really very few bikes in that  country? There’s plenty of mass transit.   There’s lots of walking. Many of the streets  are walking-friendly. Bikes hardly play a role. MARS: I think that’s a little bit of the  culture. The good thing is the pressure   release valve that they created was extremely  effective. Beautiful public transit system. I   love being in Tokyo. It makes me feel great  because I just love the ability to get anywhere   and do anything like that. If it serves that way,  then that’s great. If we have a patchy network,   then coming up with cheap ways to get between  them, whether it be e-bikes, or really buses,   is also the secret to public transit that  people don’t employ as much as they should   probably because they’re not as sexy as  cool trains. Those types of things, I think,   are important to putting together a patchy network  that isn’t as devised as well as it could be. COWEN: I sometimes hear the  claim that internationally,   current design trends are leading  us toward a kind of placelessness,   that these coffee shops look the  same in Bangkok, Tokyo, Paris,   Buenos Aires. I’m not sure it’s true, but what’s  your opinion? It’s not obviously wrong, right? MARS: No, it’s not obviously wrong, but you do  feel it. I think there’s another thing at work   here, which is a corporate globalism does create  a brand style and aesthetic that’s carried over   in places, and there can be a soullessness to that  thing as it’s transported from place to place.   I think if you’re an astute traveler and observer  of things, you notice the little differences of   things. I’m not a big McDonald’s eater, but I  do like to go to the local McDonald’s to see   whatever weird thing is on the menu that I’ve  never seen before. You can find these little   nuances and strange things in places, and you  can find them in your coffee shops and stuff. There’s a flattening of culture as you become  more global. There’s a flattening of accents   as you become more global. There’s  a flattening of all kinds of things.   I think that’s hard to deny, but I do think that   the little differences are there and present,  and they’re worth paying attention to. COWEN: Now, when the iPhone first  came out, and I bought one on day one,   I thought it looked quite beautiful.  Now, to me, it looks quite boring.   Have I changed? Did it change? Am I just too used  to it? Has it gotten worse? What’s your opinion? MARS: I think you’ve just gotten used to it.  Style trends and what we care about in design,   they do evolve. You do get bored of seeing  the same thing, and there’s an impulse to   change. Just like when we talked about with the  Chrysler Building, the idea of that ornamentation   feeling of the old era and people just loving  the sleekness of these new modern skyscrapers and   loving just the whole utility of them and the  utility represented the form. They were in love   with that, and they were in love with it for  good reasons, too. I think mostly good reasons. When you grow up in a world in which ornamentation  is reserved for the lucky few and everyone else   gets nothing, all of a sudden, ornamentation seems  offensive. You see this thing, and you go, “God,   it’s so beautiful. The function is so lovely.  You can give it to a chimpanzee, and they’ll   know how to use an iPhone.” It’s a stunning  achievement in design. Then you get used to it,   and you’re like, “You know what? A button  would be nice here or there or something.” The new one seems to be like the clamshell. It  opens up like a phone, it gives you more real   estate, but it’s seamless looking. I think that  seems to be the next one I see people being into.   For a while, that’ll seem very futuristic.  I remember the first cellphone I got was—not   the first one, but one of the early ones where I  was picking something out because of its beauty—a   Motorola Razr phone. The sleekness  of it, I thought, was just stunning,   honestly. Trends change and people  adapt. That’s the way it is. COWEN: They’re more robust now.  You can drop them, even throw them,   put them under water, they’re fine. I  worry that maybe they look less sleek   in the service of robustness. Now, I  would prefer the robustness, in fact. MARS: I think I would err toward robustness rather  than sleekness as well. The funny thing about the   phone is that being a phone is  its least important quality.   What you need out of a pocket computer versus  what you need out of a phone are different things,   and they’re diverging more all the time. As  the functionality of the iPhone is quite wide,   which is why the screen is so nice for  dealing with all that different functionality,   you’ll see things differentiate as you want  them to be more of a thing versus another. You see there’s a minor trend of  people ditching smartphones for   what they would call “dumb phones,” which function  better as a phone, where the phone is the primary   function that you’re trying to create for.  That’ll happen as you add more functionality.   These things will start to split into  different devices maybe again. You never know. COWEN: What’s the ugliest country you’ve been to? MARS: Oh, my goodness. Ugliest country. I  don’t have a candidate for ugliest country   because countries are really different. I  was in Bali recently. Bali is beautiful:   a beautiful, lovely place; beautiful, lovely  people. But I was in some of the cities,   so much of getting around is on little bikes and  motorcycles and stuff, and I’m a walker. It is   very hard to get around walking in different  cities in Bali. The gutters are right there.   There are often like a cut in the ground. It’s  pretty dangerous. You can be forced into them.   There’s just an assault on your senses and a  constant vigilance that’s required to get around. That felt ugly to me when I was there, in  parts of the country. Other parts of the   country were it’s a gorgeous, amazing place. It  was that lack of care for the type of person who   doesn’t have a car or doesn’t have a driver.  I found that uglier than I wanted it to be. COWEN: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia is quite ugly to me— MARS: I’ve never been. COWEN: —and it doesn’t have the  excuse of being poor, right? MARS: Yes. COWEN: Very poor countries, they just can’t do  certain things. Riyadh is just awful, I felt. MARS: I’ve never been there,  so I’ll take your word for it. COWEN: You should go for this reason. MARS: To experience ugliness firsthand? COWEN: Yes.   One of my favorite topics, currency design. What’s  your favorite currency in terms of how it looks? MARS: Favorite? It’s like   I love almost any of them with the US currency  in dead last. I find things to love about them.   I’ve done a story on Australian currency,  which was one of the early polymer notes.   I just like utility in currency. I like different  sizes. I like different colors. I like the fact   that they put on artists and people of note  that are not founding fathers and presidents   and stuff like this. I don’t know if I have a  particular favorite, but I was entranced by the   thoughtfulness and utility of Australian  currency when I did a story about it. You   could be blind and know what note you’re holding  because of the size. They stand up pretty well,   and they care about all kinds of things  rather than just presidents and stuff. COWEN: I loved Swiss currency pre-2021. They  had Le Corbusier on, Giacometti, Honegger. In   the 1980s, they had Euler on, the mathematician.  Imagine putting Euler on your country’s currency. MARS: That is a canvas that’s so available to  us to represent more values than we have in   the United States than just founding  fathers and presidents and stuff.   I think it’s just such a wasted opportunity. COWEN: I like the dollar, though. I’m surprised  you’re so negative. I like the weird esotericism:   the eye, the pyramid. The design is bizarre.  It announces to the world: “We’re crazy.” MARS: There are things to love about it. I  just think that its fussiness and filigree,   we’re locked in, I think for important  reasons, which is because the dollar is   the most important currency in the  world, to which all other currencies are   pegged, and therefore you don’t change  it lightly. You have to be very,   very careful. It really locked it into amber  in a way that is both beautiful to admire,   but also really limits its utility as things  move on, we get better things than linen-paper   hybrids and especially different sizes and utility  for people with different needs. I think that’s   important. There’s definitely things to love  about the dollar. The dollar has some charm. COWEN: I like the arrogance of it also. A sense  of we don’t need to make the denominations look   so different. If you’re a foreigner, we expect  you’ll come here a lot, you’ll master dollars.   Maybe you use them in your home country as  well. They don’t need to be different colors. MARS: It is definitely a bold  statement that you’re going to   adapt to our way of being if you’re  going to use the dollar, for sure. COWEN: Should America put  its power lines underground? MARS: Probably, yes. Especially in this  world of climate change and more fires.   Some of the biggest fires in California were  started by downed power lines, and that wouldn’t   happen if they were underground. That would be  really useful. I think it also just would be   prettier. I like it when they are underground too. Again, it’s mainly a cost benefit if you  can make it work. One of the things that   is good is you can run a power line to something  and you can put something up pretty quick.   That’s an amazing thing that we have a network  grid like that. If everything had to wait for   a channel to be dug underground, I think things  would be harder to build and building is of   premium importance. It’s really a  matter of balancing those things. COWEN: How should we signal especially  large speed bumps in the road?   Big issue in Virginia, where I live. MARS: Really? You just run across  them and then hit them too hard? COWEN: I live in the suburbs. Over time, the  number of them goes up, the size of them goes   up. It rarely goes down. It’s an asymmetric  process. You don’t always know what’s coming. MARS: Signage. I think we do get immune  and blind to signage after a while. I   think the road markers, like when you  have the chevrons that go over them,   help some indication, but I don’t think  they really give you a full sense of what   it is. I think your unbalance and  unsureness is almost their goal,   to make you not certain how to go over them, and  so therefore you go over them very, very slowly. COWEN: Or you could say, “I go over them  pretty quickly because I know it’s not a   credible warning. The incentive is to put up that  it’s really big and then not have it be that big.” MARS: Yes, but uncertainty seems to be its  goal, which is important in traffic devices   sometimes. Uncertainty is a good thing  because it makes people more cautious. COWEN: It’s like traffic circles. MARS: Traffic circles, for example.  I’m a big fan of the traffic circle,   and it’s all built on anxiety  as its central principle. COWEN: How should we signal  the presence of atomic waste,   knowing it will still be there thousands  of years from now or however long?   What should we put up that people  will understand in the distant future? MARS: This is a real conundrum because   there’s this chance that no language or warnings  would make sense. There was a project of this,   the WIPP program, to try to figure out how  to signal people that were basically almost   nonhuman in their evolution in terms of what  to warn them against these things. They ran   into this problem that seems very fundamental and  hard to conceive of. Even putting a pictogram of   a person, they run into a contact of radioactive  material, and then—a three-panel comic strip of   a person who is healthy runs into radioactive  material—and the next panel shows them sick or   dying. We don’t even know if people will perceive  a left-to-right orientation in our picture. You really have to come up with novel ways  to make these things persistent over time.   People have thought about creating folk songs.  They’ve thought about putting radioactive   responsive markers in animals and releasing  them, so like radioactive cats. If a cat was   around radioactive material, they would glow, and  then build a folk tradition around it that the   glowing cats are things to avoid and maybe that  persistent story would last over millennia.   It’s an interesting and confounding problem, but  people came up with really creative solutions. I think it’s evidenced by  what we did when we discovered   different tombs in Egypt and stuff. There’s  no amount of warning that will stop a person   who’s determined to get into a place, even if it  seems intimidating or has traps or whatever it is.   It just makes us more motivated. It’s an  actual problem to think about, for sure. COWEN: Or you might think there’s  some kind of treasure there, and   they’re trying to scare you  off because it’s valuable. MARS: Exactly. There’s no way to convey  100 percent what you mean because   places that are protected seem like  there’s something valuable behind it,   and in this case there’s nothing valuable. COWEN: A related problem: When you’re  coming off the highway, as you well know,   typically you have to go more slowly  on the ramp. If you ought to be going,   say, 40 on the ramp, they’ll tell you ought to  be going 25. Should they just tell us the truth,   or should they systematically lie to us  and say 25, even though 37 might be okay? MARS: I don’t know. That type of  misinformation—very early on in   my driving career, I learned that 10 miles above  the suggested limit was what they were going for. COWEN: Usually. Yes. MARS: I think there’s some utility in me figuring  that out and doing the math as I become a better   driver or a more confident driver or know  the roads better that serves some purpose.   It’s just that that purpose, like  the intention and the effect are   hard to calculate. Would it be better  to tell people the truth? Maybe. COWEN: Another rule is to double  the number and subtract 10,   if that’s more ambitious in your system. MARS: There is a lot of driving, at least traffic  devices, and driving in general on the highway in   particular, is all designed around calming your  brain so that you will go that fast because   humans are not evolved to go that fast. If you  were to get out on a highway and stand next to a   sign, most people marvel at the size of a highway  sign. They have no idea that it’s really that big.   Part of that and the dashes in between lanes,  most people estimate when surveyed that a dash   in the dividing line of a highway is two feet  long, when in fact they’re 10 to 15 feet long. It is all there to calm your  brain at going at high speeds   so that you can go very fast and have it not  freak you out. When you’re going to transition to   tricking people’s brains into going very fast  so that a highway functions, you have to do   things that shock people out of their hypnotic  state to get them into a different driving mode.   An artificially low speed limit or suggested  limit, it makes some sense to do it that way.   Also, as people begin to game it and know what’s  going on, obviously it starts to feel ridiculous. COWEN: You have a very famous TED Talk on city  flags and what makes for a good city flag.   You’ve propagated the term  “vexillology,” the study of flags.   Why should there be no lettering  on flags? City flags, that is. MARS: Because a flag is meant to be flying  on a pole, and so it should be seen.   It should effectively work  from backwards and forwards.   It’s just because it has a backside  that you can see, and so it’s not good. COWEN: What about the other perspective, that  outsiders never see flags? I’ve been, I think,   to the 50 largest American  cities. Often, repeatedly,   there’s not one city flag I could identify  from any one of them until I saw your talk. MARS: You could identify Chicago  flag if you’ve been to Chicago. COWEN: No, I couldn’t. MARS: Really? COWEN: I absolutely couldn’t. MARS: Oh, it’s everywhere in  Chicago. That’s interesting. COWEN: Maybe the purpose of the flag is  to signal to interest groups internally   that they’re respected by the city  or the mayor or the government.   Then you want some lettering.  It looks ugly, but who cares? MARS: My contention in that talk was, a little  bit, I was just making fun and having fun with   the idea of the design of flags. In general,  what I was discovering as I was thinking   about this was that when cities have good  flags, they use them well and they’re very,   very useful as a municipal device. Chicago is  one of those examples where the Chicago flag is   displayed everywhere and different elements of  it are taken apart and presented. It actually   reinforces and feeds Chicago pride in,  I think, a meaningful and important way. When you’re in a place that has an  effective flag, usually because it   adheres to these guidelines that Ted Kaye  laid out in his vexillology handbook,   it has this positive reinforcement effect, this  positive feedback loop of having pride in the   city, in displaying a good-looking flag. You  want to display it because it’s good-looking,   it gives you more pride in the place. It  has this nice effect. I think that’s useful   and good. The way to make a good designed  flag is to follow basic principles this way. If you can love a flag that has lots of colors,  and it’s really busy, and has words on it,   and that gives you the same amount of  pride and has the same amount of utility,   absolutely fine. I’m not there to police  that part of it. I was just giving people   the idea of the tools to make a flag loved because  it is an underused thing in a city to rally around   to give people pride other than sports teams and  other corporate things. This is a thing that we   all own. It’s a piece of design and branding that  is a lovely thing to embrace if it’s beautiful   enough to embrace. That’s the pathway to it is to  make it so that it works in a lot of instances. Taking words off of it is one of the  things that I think is a good idea. I   think it makes for a cleaner, more beautiful  thing. There’s examples in which—mostly   words I don’t like at all—but there’s examples  in which things that violate flag rules   are, in lovely and amazing ways, that I think  is really beautiful. I think Maryland’s flag   is really beautiful and it harkens back to the  heraldry of Lord Baltimore and Calvert. It’s super   busy and it looks like a racing flag. I think  it’s super gorgeous. You can do it lots of ways. COWEN: The Brazilian flag, it’s “Ordem  e Progresso,” or “Order and Progress,”   which sometimes is taken almost  satirically, but I quite like it. MARS: I think the Brazilian flag is great. That’s  another place where they really embrace it. That’s   really it. My goal or my hope for places is just  that recognized flags can be really beautiful.   They’re worth the effort to make them so. They’re  worth lauding and flying. I have a flagpole at   my house. I love putting out flags for various  independence days around the world and various   things that are happening in my life. If I’m going  to visit someplace, I’ll sometimes put a flag up   beforehand. I just think that they’re great  and worth spending some time thinking about.   If it has little words on it, so be it.  The Brazilian flag is an amazing flag. COWEN: You almost convinced me that  Pocatello, Idaho has the best flag   in the country rather than the worst. I  agree with everything you say about it,   but there’s otherwise no chance you and I  would be mentioning Pocatello, Idaho, right? MARS: Yes. That’s the thing. I went there to  talk to them about their flag. I called them   out as having the worst flag. The NAVA  survey identified it as the worst flag   in the country. I called them out in this TED  Talk. I was really just having fun with it.   They got in touch. They wanted to redesign the  flag. The truth of the matter is that flag;   it was only official flag in the barest sense.  It was a branding that meant for municipal cars   and things like that, and then they put it on a  flag. They presented it as their official flag,   but it wasn’t made for that. There’s evidence that  it wasn’t made for that because it has a trademark   symbol on it. It has things on it that you  wouldn’t put on a flag, but it was put on a flag. Then I went to visit them as they were doing  a redesign. I met one of the city leaders.   He was like, “I have to thank you for this because   it would be the worst if we were the  second-worst flag in the country,” then,   “That would be so much worse than being the  absolute worst because then we have motivation   to change, and we had people talking about it, and  it was really fun. The process of figuring out a   new flag was so much fun.” They had a really  good spirit about it. I was very grateful.   They took it really well. I really meant  no harm. It was a fun moment in the talk. Since that TED Talk has been out, there  have been something in the neighborhood of   250 or 300 municipal flag redesigns in the  country. I think it was just this moment   to just take a look at our place, know that we’re  part of this thing, and make something that we’re   proud of. Even if at the end of it, they go, “You  know what? We love the thing that we had,” that’s   totally fine. I’m happy with it. I like that  people were thinking about it in terms of a city   because I like that as an organizing principle  of people’s lives and their sense of pride. I love sports, too, like overall sports  teams. Our office was in Oakland downtown   for a long time and our sports teams left.  You can count on Oakland to be Oakland,   but you can’t necessarily count on the A’s being  here or the Warriors playing in the stadium here. COWEN: How well designed is your  own studio by your own account? MARS: My own studio? COWEN: Your own studio. MARS: I like it. There’s a little closet that  was meant to be a utility closet in my house,   and then they realized that they could put the  water heater somewhere in a crawlspace in another   part of the house, and they had it open. As soon  as I was touring it when I was going to buy it,   I walked in, I was like, “I know exactly  what this room is going to be.” It became   my studio instantly. I have this—it’s called  Cityscape—audio-dampening material that me and my   stepdaughter put up over a couple of days. Then I  actually have still images—that’s the cover of my   book—but it’s done in Softscape, so it dampens  the sound. Yes, I love my studio. It’s great. I have a standing desk, so I stand all day.   It’s perfectly meant for me. My house is not  the greatest place to put a studio inside of   because it’s a pretty open-plan house. I  have a wife and six children live here,   or at least they did when they mostly lived  here, and now they mostly live in colleges   around the country. I can hear everything in the  house, so it’s not perfect in that sense. If they   turn on a faucet in the kitchen, I can hear it.  Other than that, I love my studio. It’s great. COWEN: What do you think are the  advantages of doing a podcast or   radio show about visual objects,  but the show itself is audio only? MARS: I think it has to do with overcoming  people’s biases. If I show you a building, I   think you have a reaction to the building because  of what you’re exposed to and what you like and   don’t like, and for all kinds of reasons, good and  bad. If I could tell you the story of a building,   I can make you fall in love with it. Then you see  it, and then all of a sudden you see the merits,   usually in its function, over your  initial take on its aesthetics. I think that there’s something about when  I was developing the show 16, 17 years ago,   I was really into that idea of telling the  story of design versus having people react   to the visuals of design, and that it told  a different story that was nice and needed   to be told about intentionality and the things  that we make and do and surround ourselves with. COWEN: Now, you’ve been extremely productive,  and for a long period of time, in the worlds   of podcast, radio, and also writing. What do you  think is your most unusual successful work habit? MARS: Huh. Unusual? COWEN: If you said, “Oh, I wake up early  every morning,” not everyone does it,   but it’s not unusual, right? MARS: Yes. I’m trying to  think. What would be unusual?   When I think about what I am most proud of, I love  being a producer. What I love about it is it means   everything. There’s stages of your job and life  in which you’re cutting tape, or you’re writing   stuff, or you’re reading stuff. There’s times  when you’re trying to solve a problem of what goes   on in the next episode. As my career developed,  I became a producer. My job was to keep a cohort   of people happy and productive, and managing them  in a way where their talents are brought forward. I loved solving the problem of funding the  show and making sure everyone got paid,   so all those things that I think people  think they’ll go like, “Was it bad when you   could no longer do stories and you ran a  business?” I was like, “I loved it. I loved   each part of it.” The unusual part is I think  I was very much like a leaf on the wind when it   came to what my job, how it changed over time,  and being very content in each of those roles. I think that’s the key to my success is taking  what is going on in the world, adapting to it,   and really thinking about solving the problem  of putting a show on the air every week,   and thinking of it as a total  problem. No part of it is   outside of my scope. No part of it is too  small to bear attention. I think that’s it.   I don’t think that’s unusual necessarily.  I think that’s the secret to my success. The other part of my success is I try to lead  with kindness first. The people who work with me,   like Delaney Hall is our senior editor on 99PI.  I hired Delaney out of college in 2005. We’ve   worked together in different parts. She’s gone to  another show and come back. I think I’ve created   a culture where the people work together, are kind  and tender with each other. That’s a thing that I   think is really, really important to making a  thing because we make a thing that’s an expression   of art and what we care about and what we notice  in the world. I think that only is achieved when   people’s personalities are there, and they’re  feeling their best and they’re feeling supported. COWEN: Great answer. Roman  Mars, thank you very much. MARS: Thank you so much for  having me. It’s been fun.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,
I am speaking with design expert Roman Mars. He is  the host and creator of the podcast 99% Invisible,
which he describes as a sound-rich narrative  podcast, and it’s about the unnoticed
architectural and design choices that shape our  world. It is one of the most listened-to podcasts,
and it now has over 500 million downloads. He also  has an excellent book, The 99% Invisible City:
A Field Guide to the Hidden World of Everyday  Design, also with Kurt Kohlstedt. Roman, welcome.
ROMAN MARS: Oh, thank you so much for  having me. It’s a pleasure to be here.
COWEN: I have many design  questions for you. Let’s start.
MARS: I hope I have design answers for you.
COWEN: This, I think, is a hard one because  I found it hard, but where do you think
in the world the street signs are the most  attractive, and what makes them that way?
MARS: Oh, my Lord. I don’t know if I know a  good answer for this. I’d be happy to hear
your answer. What I find, mostly as I’m getting  older, is that the most beautiful street signs are
the ones I can see the best. I’m always confounded  by the fact that, especially as a pedestrian,
street signs are often, the vantage point that  they’re really concerned about is a driver versus
a walker. As a walker, you’ll find that the  street sign is placed before the intersection,
that it’s for the driver approaching. You’ll be  on a corner and you’ll be looking around New York,
and you’re like, “I don’t know where I  am,” because it’s a little bit behind you.
Yes, I don’t know if I have a favorite, like  really beautiful one in particular, but I do love
a really good grid. I like a street that  you know how to navigate without too
much looking at your phone. That makes me  very happy. I also love to get lost in the
alleys of Venice too. You just have to forge  ahead, and you’ll get there eventually.
COWEN: Venice has good street signs, but  for size, I would go with Los Angeles.
MARS: Yes, they’re quite big.
COWEN: They’re designed for drivers.
I think for quality, most people would say some  mix of Spain and Portugal, which have these
ceramic themes. They’re not my favorites,  but they would be classic choices.
MARS: I’ve only been to Spain a little  bit. Yes, they’re really quite beautiful.
There’s an abundance of good choices,  but to me, it’s about functionality.
COWEN: I like the more artistic Switzerland, where  there’s just the name and a color, and there’s
blue and green, and it tells you how big a street  or highway it will be, and everything is stark and
it’s in this very Swiss font. That’s my personal  favorite, but I don’t think it would win a poll.
MARS: It just matters if it works for you.
COWEN: Yes. Here’s another question I’ve  thought about: Why is it that older cars,
maybe most classically from the early 1960s,  but not only, they’re so much more attractive
than today. Today, so many cars are SUVs, they  look literally the same. They’re so boring.
They’re not offensive, but in the aggregate,  maybe they’re offensive. What happened?
MARS: This is confounding to me. I’ve talked to  a lot of industrial designers and designers over
the years, and cars are often the way they got  into design, caring about design as kids. That’s
the first thing they ever noticed and really loved  and cared about. A lot of it has to do with those
forms that were so bold; it was a  game on the highway where you could
look ahead of you and from just the shape, you  could say what model and make of car, maybe
what year of car. It was so distinctive. Now,  I think you couldn’t do that at all as a game.
I think that there’s boring and plain reasons for  this, which are just energy resources and things.
We put a lot of steel unnecessarily in cars during  our extractive phase of manufacturing, where we
made big and bold choices because we didn’t care  that the things got 10 miles to the gallon and
the shapes of the fins and the structures were  ridiculously unsafe for the people inside.
Those get shaved down by necessity and the  needs of the environment, the needs of society.
Then I think that there’s something about  people gravitating toward a mean and trying
to mass-produce something that appeals to  the biggest number of people, and then it
gets increasingly more and more  same-y. I do think it’s a real shame.
The moments where there are all these breakout  moments of something looking really different,
I have to admit, I don’t really like  them necessarily when they do. I think
the Cybertruck is a horrible-looking  vehicle, but it looks a lot different,
mainly because its utility is quite terrible.  Yes, it’s a real risk to go far afield and try
to create something brand new. I think there’s  a few pressures working to make things the same.
COWEN: Do you find Waymos attractive? Because I  do. They look different. They look futuristic.
MARS: Because of all the gadgetry on top?
COWEN: The whirring thing on top. It’s almost  satire how they look, but I enjoy it. I smile.
MARS: I’ve never been in a Waymo. This is my own  personal thing: This is getting very personal
very fast, but my one recurring nightmare  when I’m very, very stressed is I’m in the
backseat of a car with nobody driving, and I’m  trying to climb over to control the vehicle.
They’re not made for me in that sense because I  feel like if I was choosing to make that choice.
But Waymos seem very great. I think studies  are very clear that a robot-driving car is
way better than a human-driving car, so  I have no problem personally with them.
COWEN: Do you think the nightmare  goes away if you confront it?
MARS: Maybe. I think there’s a chance of that. It  is my one recurring thing is being in a speeding,
uncontrolled car, and I have to climb  over from the backseat to control it.
COWEN: Now, I grew up in New Jersey, where we  have what’s sometimes called the panhandle.
MARS: Jughandles.
COWEN: Jughandles, as a way of making left turns.  You go around and then through from the side.
Do you feel we underuse those, or  should even New Jersey not have them?
MARS: There’s some good thought and efficiency  built into jughandles. The problem is they really
only work if you know they’re coming.  If you’re familiar with the streets,
it is a nice thing of avoiding long left  turns or people waiting to make left turns.
If you don’t know the street, like  I’ve driven around in Jersey a lot,
and it’s just you don’t know if you  should be on the left or the right.
I’m a driver who likes to be in the lane I’m  in very, very early. Making a rapid decision
realizing that, all of a sudden, that you’re  going to have to make a right to make a left is
something that also just really stresses me out.  If it was consistently used and there were never
lefts, I’d be all for it. It’s the inconsistency  which I think is a little bit of a problem.
COWEN: Maybe no one really  visits New Jersey, right?
You wouldn’t do it in California or  Florida where plenty of people visit.
MARS: Yes, that’s true. It is definitely  made for the people who are there.
COWEN: People in New Jersey, they don’t even  visit other parts of New Jersey unless it’s
what they call the New Jersey Shore. Only in  New Jersey do they call it the shore, right?
MARS: Fair enough. COWEN: Not beach, it’s the shore.
MARS: That’s right.
COWEN: Thus it may work there. I worry  that as the value of land goes up,
the jughandle or panhandle, it takes up more land.
MARS: It certainly does. UPS has algorithms  where they make sure their drivers never make a
left turn because it is just so inefficient and so  bad for their routes. I’m of that belief. I’ll go
way around the block to make sure I’m not making  a left in a place that I’m not confident making
a left. I think the jughandle does serve a real  good purpose. It’s just the amount that has to be
telegraphed to a person not familiar with them  means that its utility is somewhat diminished.
COWEN: What do you think of yellow  lighting on our roads? When I was a kid,
that was a trend for a while. I never  saw it take off. Is there any advantage?
MARS: Yellow lighting, like as  in the overhead streetlights?
COWEN: Instead of white.
MARS: I don’t really know what the advantage is. I  haven’t really thought about it too much. I think
getting things toward more natural light and less  glaring light is important in terms of our sense
of the world and how much we want to engage with  the night sky and stuff like that. As long as it’s
thoughtful in terms of light pollution, mostly  it’s a good thing, but I’m not quite sure in
this case. I did interview a group of designers  who had a company called Civil Twilight, and it
was all about making streetlights a little bit  more responsive, a little less glaring, allowing
us to have a little bit more vision of the night  sky in our cities. I’m all for that type of thing.
COWEN: What color should the central stripe be?
MARS: On a road?
COWEN: On a road, yes. Just white?
MARS: I think the utility makes sense.  It’s white on the outside, it’s yellow
on the inside if you don’t want it to cross,  like double line if you don’t want to cross.
I think that’s pretty good. I like  the cat’s eyes reflective little
markers that I think help me out a lot, again,  as my vision is not as good as it used to be.
I really rely on these retroreflective  paints and cat’s eye, different things
to make it so that I can see them. That’s the  most important thing is being able to see them.
COWEN: Now, if I think of small towns in New  England, many are quite charming or beautiful.
If I think of Houston, not that much of  it is attractive to me. Yet, Houston is
growing pretty rapidly and the small towns are  shrinking. How should I interpret that trend?
MARS: Houston is a place famously with no zoning  laws whatsoever. That does create a type of growth
that is valuable to some. I think it has its  limits. What it does is it creates car culture,
which is, I think, a net negative  to only build a city around a car.
COWEN: If it’s a net negative,  why is everyone moving there? Or
like northern Florida, which is also car  culture, growing rapidly in population?
MARS: Definitely when you  ease those burdens of growth,
growth is easier. I think that’s pretty clear.  Then when growth is easier, cost is down.
It’s all about making choices. I think  that there’s going to be a group of people
that find that to be perfectly great and  perfectly that’s the world that they want,
and there’s enough populace in the United States  and a heterogeneity of what they care about that
that’ll be attractive, and then there’ll be places  where that’s not attractive. There’s definitely
enough population to support it regardless, and so  it’s fine that they have a place to go, for sure.
COWEN: Can you see a world coming, just say in the  United States, where actually where people live
becomes more attractive on average and we build  new things, maybe in different styles, but they’re
attractive as small New England towns might be  attractive, and the country overall, the living
structures become more beautiful? Is there a  path toward that, or is that just impossible now?
MARS: No, it’s not impossible. I do think  these things change and our sense of them
of what is attractive and what isn’t will  modify us over time. I do think there’s real
care and design in new structures. I’ve definitely  seen them in places that I’ve visited. I
was in New York recently. I think the best example  of this is London, which has a lot of historic
buildings, and the integration with the new modern  buildings, often inside of the same building, is
gorgeous. Really, really well done. There’s a  way to do it so that there’s a harmony amongst
these things. I think it has to do with the  trends in cities and what they’re going for.
There’s a habit of care that is  retained. When you go to Chicago
and you see all the skyscrapers, there was an  onus on each of the different architectural firms
to have the skyscrapers talk to each other, even  across decades. I think it was a cultural thing,
not just about money or economics or something  like that. I think there was just a sense that the
Trump International Hotel, it had these different  levels, and one of those levels is the exact same
height as the Wrigley Building, and the next  level is the height of the next building around.
It has these things that speak to  the area, that speak to beauty.
I think there’s something about them  that there’s a culture of that can
be retained and brought forward. I think  it’s present. I think there’s definitely
ways to make things beautiful and  continue to make things beautiful.
COWEN: Would you say, is there any residential  neighborhood, take just the United States,
post-World War II, that you would say is beautiful  in the same way you would say Shaker Heights
is beautiful or some suburbs of Chicago are  beautiful? Because I can’t think of one, frankly.
MARS: I can’t think of a beautiful suburb.
COWEN: Now, I would say parts of Copenhagen  are quite new and beautiful, parts of Helsinki,
but there’s not much in the Western world.  In the US, I can’t think of anything.
MARS: I don’t know if I can think of  something off the top of my head like that.
COWEN: You’re a design expert. I’m not  criticizing you. I’m agreeing with you.
What has gone wrong with us?  What’s your account of this?
MARS: I think it’s just about what  people want. I think a little bit of
the cohesion and harmony of a place
has to do with proximity and putting things close  together and people noticing. When you have places
that are further apart, like buildings, even  just houses that are further apart, and you have
the pressures of industrial manufacturing—housing  is one of those things that economists and people
thinking about it have always tried to  make it cheaper and cheaper and cheaper,
and in a way, it has a speed of light that they  can’t quite crack because building is local.
They try to make things more modular.  They try to make it more cookie cutter.
At a certain point, they just can’t break through  a certain level. I was talking to Stephen Dubner
from Freakonomics about this at one point.  We were discussing this idea. I was like,
“I don’t want building to get more efficient.  I want it to be inefficient in ways because I
want people to make individual decisions and I  want local workers to be paid a certain amount
of money.” I think there’s an impulse to push  things to be more uniform and, I think, in a way,
less beautiful, but there’ll always be those  pockets where beauty and good design can be found.
I think these things shift back and  forth in terms of what people care about
and just a matter of finding the right  collection of people that are willing to
put up with it at a level of  inefficiency to pay for the beauty.
COWEN: Why wasn’t the Chrysler  Building more popular at first?
MARS: It landed at a time period of the upswing of  modernism. It has all these, what are considered
at the time to be garish adornments, like the  silver hubcaps and the eagles and things to evoke
cars like the Chrysler. Modernists, especially  architecture critics at the time, were like,
“Oh, this is silly filigree on this building.”  I think it’s gorgeous. I love that building.
COWEN: Same here.
MARS: Its harsh criticism  and was a victim of the era.
Since then, I think it’s endured, and that’s why  it’s great to have buildings around for a while to
have them reassessed. Most of the buildings  that I’ve ever done stories about have been
reassessed over and over and over again.  You just have to be there long enough.
COWEN: Do you enjoy brutalism?
MARS: I do. Again, it’s something that it can  be done right or it can be done wrong. I think
one of the things about brutalism, why it appeals  to invested architecture fans and architects is,
in the abstract, the shapes and the forms are  really beautiful, especially as a drawing.
I think what brutalism fails is that it  doesn’t age particularly well because the
way the concrete aggregate, it can fall apart,  it can get cracked, it can feel heavy and
just intense. There’s places where  that brutalism form makes things
just oppressive and feel inhuman, and there’s  places where it feels extremely human and lovely.
I love the Barbican in London. I think there’s a
functionality to that place that’s really  gorgeous, and the shapes of it are gorgeous.
You can do it well and then you can do  it in ways that are shocking to people.
COWEN: Which do you think are cities that  do a good job incorporating greenery?
MARS: I think that all of them
have gone through phases where they really  cared and where they haven’t. One of the
things I think about when it comes to New  York City in particular, I just think that
everyone should take a minute, all the time,  to recognize the miracle of Central Park.
The most expensive real estate in the world,  probably, for much of its time in existence
was held off to create this space  for people and that that place was
revolutionized through Olmsted; revolutionized  in the sense of what we treat parks and how
they speak to nature in a real way. That’s  just a stunning achievement to me. I think
of that. I live in the Bay Area. Golden Gate Park,  similarly, the existence of it is stunning to me.
COWEN: Would Paris be better if  it had such a park? Because you’d
be pushing out a lot of Parisians.
MARS: Yes. Probably. When you make  those decisions long ago, it’s easier to
value those decisions. If you were to raze a  whole neighborhood to the ground, several blocks,
it would be a harder ROI to calculate. I do think  that green spaces and public gathering spaces are
extremely important to a city, and when they  don’t have them, they suffer greatly for them.
COWEN: What did Jane Jacobs get wrong?
MARS: There’s a dichotomy that people draw  of the Jane Jacobs versus the Robert Moses
style of bottom-up versus top-down.  I do think that Jane Jacobs’ sense
of what a city or neighborhood should and could be  coming from the ground up is extremely astute and
on the money. I think her sense of the sidewalk  ballet and all those things are really important,
and they’re keen observations. I do think  that, taken to an extreme, there is a sense
that there is no good from top-down  planning, and I actually think that there is.
I think that a functioning city operates both  top-down and bottom-up, and they both listen to
each other and they make big plans. There’s  not a lot of room in the Jacobs’ worldview,
in the extreme, for top-down plans that  really do matter and are effective and
make the world a better place. There can be  a historic preservationist streak in that,
a NIMBYism inside of Jane Jacobs that  I think could have a pernicious effect.
It isn’t present in her writing, but I think that  the natural follow-through has that potential.
COWEN: What would she have thought of e-bike  lanes, which we now have a lot of in many places?
MARS: I don’t know. Do they contribute to  the sidewalk ballet? I’m going to guess.
I’m going to say a little bit no and a little  bit yes. I don’t know how she would land on
e-bikes. I don’t know. It’s a good question.
COWEN: What’s your view? Do they make cities  uglier or more attractive? I would say uglier.
MARS: The e-bike lanes in  particular or just the e-bikes?
COWEN: Both, if you have the lanes.
MARS: I think that streets do need to be reclaimed  as a place of multimodal transportation, not just
given over to cars. I think that’s a good impulse.  The street existed in human history as a place for
humans, and horses, and carts, and eventually  cars, and then a change came and then they were
just only for cars and you were at fault if you  were a human inside of that street if anything
went wrong. I think that making streets more  flexible, more multimodal is a good impulse.
I think the bikes are fine, I think the lanes are  fine as long as they work well. I think they’re
important toward deconstructing the hegemony of a  car. I think a car is a good thing. I have a car.
I like it. It’s good in some environments.  It’s not ideal for cities in a lot of ways.
It’s important to have different ways  to break apart the mobility of a city.
COWEN: The land costs a lot. What do you  think of the Tokyo and Japanese model
where there’s really very few bikes in that  country? There’s plenty of mass transit.
There’s lots of walking. Many of the streets  are walking-friendly. Bikes hardly play a role.
MARS: I think that’s a little bit of the  culture. The good thing is the pressure
release valve that they created was extremely  effective. Beautiful public transit system. I
love being in Tokyo. It makes me feel great  because I just love the ability to get anywhere
and do anything like that. If it serves that way,  then that’s great. If we have a patchy network,
then coming up with cheap ways to get between  them, whether it be e-bikes, or really buses,
is also the secret to public transit that  people don’t employ as much as they should
probably because they’re not as sexy as  cool trains. Those types of things, I think,
are important to putting together a patchy network  that isn’t as devised as well as it could be.
COWEN: I sometimes hear the  claim that internationally,
current design trends are leading  us toward a kind of placelessness,
that these coffee shops look the  same in Bangkok, Tokyo, Paris,
Buenos Aires. I’m not sure it’s true, but what’s  your opinion? It’s not obviously wrong, right?
MARS: No, it’s not obviously wrong, but you do  feel it. I think there’s another thing at work
here, which is a corporate globalism does create  a brand style and aesthetic that’s carried over
in places, and there can be a soullessness to that  thing as it’s transported from place to place.
I think if you’re an astute traveler and observer  of things, you notice the little differences of
things. I’m not a big McDonald’s eater, but I  do like to go to the local McDonald’s to see
whatever weird thing is on the menu that I’ve  never seen before. You can find these little
nuances and strange things in places, and you  can find them in your coffee shops and stuff.
There’s a flattening of culture as you become  more global. There’s a flattening of accents
as you become more global. There’s  a flattening of all kinds of things.
I think that’s hard to deny, but I do think that
the little differences are there and present,  and they’re worth paying attention to.
COWEN: Now, when the iPhone first  came out, and I bought one on day one,
I thought it looked quite beautiful.  Now, to me, it looks quite boring.
Have I changed? Did it change? Am I just too used  to it? Has it gotten worse? What’s your opinion?
MARS: I think you’ve just gotten used to it.  Style trends and what we care about in design,
they do evolve. You do get bored of seeing  the same thing, and there’s an impulse to
change. Just like when we talked about with the  Chrysler Building, the idea of that ornamentation
feeling of the old era and people just loving  the sleekness of these new modern skyscrapers and
loving just the whole utility of them and the  utility represented the form. They were in love
with that, and they were in love with it for  good reasons, too. I think mostly good reasons.
When you grow up in a world in which ornamentation  is reserved for the lucky few and everyone else
gets nothing, all of a sudden, ornamentation seems  offensive. You see this thing, and you go, “God,
it’s so beautiful. The function is so lovely.  You can give it to a chimpanzee, and they’ll
know how to use an iPhone.” It’s a stunning  achievement in design. Then you get used to it,
and you’re like, “You know what? A button  would be nice here or there or something.”
The new one seems to be like the clamshell. It  opens up like a phone, it gives you more real
estate, but it’s seamless looking. I think that  seems to be the next one I see people being into.
For a while, that’ll seem very futuristic.  I remember the first cellphone I got was—not
the first one, but one of the early ones where I  was picking something out because of its beauty—a
Motorola Razr phone. The sleekness  of it, I thought, was just stunning,
honestly. Trends change and people  adapt. That’s the way it is.
COWEN: They’re more robust now.  You can drop them, even throw them,
put them under water, they’re fine. I  worry that maybe they look less sleek
in the service of robustness. Now, I  would prefer the robustness, in fact.
MARS: I think I would err toward robustness rather  than sleekness as well. The funny thing about the
phone is that being a phone is  its least important quality.
What you need out of a pocket computer versus  what you need out of a phone are different things,
and they’re diverging more all the time. As  the functionality of the iPhone is quite wide,
which is why the screen is so nice for  dealing with all that different functionality,
you’ll see things differentiate as you want  them to be more of a thing versus another.
You see there’s a minor trend of  people ditching smartphones for
what they would call “dumb phones,” which function  better as a phone, where the phone is the primary
function that you’re trying to create for.  That’ll happen as you add more functionality.
These things will start to split into  different devices maybe again. You never know.
COWEN: What’s the ugliest country you’ve been to?
MARS: Oh, my goodness. Ugliest country. I  don’t have a candidate for ugliest country
because countries are really different. I  was in Bali recently. Bali is beautiful:
a beautiful, lovely place; beautiful, lovely  people. But I was in some of the cities,
so much of getting around is on little bikes and  motorcycles and stuff, and I’m a walker. It is
very hard to get around walking in different  cities in Bali. The gutters are right there.
There are often like a cut in the ground. It’s  pretty dangerous. You can be forced into them.
There’s just an assault on your senses and a  constant vigilance that’s required to get around.
That felt ugly to me when I was there, in  parts of the country. Other parts of the
country were it’s a gorgeous, amazing place. It  was that lack of care for the type of person who
doesn’t have a car or doesn’t have a driver.  I found that uglier than I wanted it to be.
COWEN: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia is quite ugly to me—
MARS: I’ve never been.
COWEN: —and it doesn’t have the  excuse of being poor, right?
MARS: Yes.
COWEN: Very poor countries, they just can’t do  certain things. Riyadh is just awful, I felt.
MARS: I’ve never been there,  so I’ll take your word for it.
COWEN: You should go for this reason.
MARS: To experience ugliness firsthand?
COWEN: Yes.
One of my favorite topics, currency design. What’s  your favorite currency in terms of how it looks?
MARS: Favorite? It’s like
I love almost any of them with the US currency  in dead last. I find things to love about them.
I’ve done a story on Australian currency,  which was one of the early polymer notes.
I just like utility in currency. I like different  sizes. I like different colors. I like the fact
that they put on artists and people of note  that are not founding fathers and presidents
and stuff like this. I don’t know if I have a  particular favorite, but I was entranced by the
thoughtfulness and utility of Australian  currency when I did a story about it. You
could be blind and know what note you’re holding  because of the size. They stand up pretty well,
and they care about all kinds of things  rather than just presidents and stuff.
COWEN: I loved Swiss currency pre-2021. They  had Le Corbusier on, Giacometti, Honegger. In
the 1980s, they had Euler on, the mathematician.  Imagine putting Euler on your country’s currency.
MARS: That is a canvas that’s so available to  us to represent more values than we have in
the United States than just founding  fathers and presidents and stuff.
I think it’s just such a wasted opportunity.
COWEN: I like the dollar, though. I’m surprised  you’re so negative. I like the weird esotericism:
the eye, the pyramid. The design is bizarre.  It announces to the world: “We’re crazy.”
MARS: There are things to love about it. I  just think that its fussiness and filigree,
we’re locked in, I think for important  reasons, which is because the dollar is
the most important currency in the  world, to which all other currencies are
pegged, and therefore you don’t change  it lightly. You have to be very,
very careful. It really locked it into amber  in a way that is both beautiful to admire,
but also really limits its utility as things  move on, we get better things than linen-paper
hybrids and especially different sizes and utility  for people with different needs. I think that’s
important. There’s definitely things to love  about the dollar. The dollar has some charm.
COWEN: I like the arrogance of it also. A sense  of we don’t need to make the denominations look
so different. If you’re a foreigner, we expect  you’ll come here a lot, you’ll master dollars.
Maybe you use them in your home country as  well. They don’t need to be different colors.
MARS: It is definitely a bold  statement that you’re going to
adapt to our way of being if you’re  going to use the dollar, for sure.
COWEN: Should America put  its power lines underground?
MARS: Probably, yes. Especially in this  world of climate change and more fires.
Some of the biggest fires in California were  started by downed power lines, and that wouldn’t
happen if they were underground. That would be  really useful. I think it also just would be
prettier. I like it when they are underground too.
Again, it’s mainly a cost benefit if you  can make it work. One of the things that
is good is you can run a power line to something  and you can put something up pretty quick.
That’s an amazing thing that we have a network  grid like that. If everything had to wait for
a channel to be dug underground, I think things  would be harder to build and building is of
premium importance. It’s really a  matter of balancing those things.
COWEN: How should we signal especially  large speed bumps in the road?
Big issue in Virginia, where I live.
MARS: Really? You just run across  them and then hit them too hard?
COWEN: I live in the suburbs. Over time, the  number of them goes up, the size of them goes
up. It rarely goes down. It’s an asymmetric  process. You don’t always know what’s coming.
MARS: Signage. I think we do get immune  and blind to signage after a while. I
think the road markers, like when you  have the chevrons that go over them,
help some indication, but I don’t think  they really give you a full sense of what
it is. I think your unbalance and  unsureness is almost their goal,
to make you not certain how to go over them, and  so therefore you go over them very, very slowly.
COWEN: Or you could say, “I go over them  pretty quickly because I know it’s not a
credible warning. The incentive is to put up that  it’s really big and then not have it be that big.”
MARS: Yes, but uncertainty seems to be its  goal, which is important in traffic devices
sometimes. Uncertainty is a good thing  because it makes people more cautious.
COWEN: It’s like traffic circles.
MARS: Traffic circles, for example.  I’m a big fan of the traffic circle,
and it’s all built on anxiety  as its central principle.
COWEN: How should we signal  the presence of atomic waste,
knowing it will still be there thousands  of years from now or however long?
What should we put up that people  will understand in the distant future?
MARS: This is a real conundrum because
there’s this chance that no language or warnings  would make sense. There was a project of this,
the WIPP program, to try to figure out how  to signal people that were basically almost
nonhuman in their evolution in terms of what  to warn them against these things. They ran
into this problem that seems very fundamental and  hard to conceive of. Even putting a pictogram of
a person, they run into a contact of radioactive  material, and then—a three-panel comic strip of
a person who is healthy runs into radioactive  material—and the next panel shows them sick or
