dying. We don’t even know if people will perceive  a left-to-right orientation in our picture.
You really have to come up with novel ways  to make these things persistent over time.
People have thought about creating folk songs.  They’ve thought about putting radioactive
responsive markers in animals and releasing  them, so like radioactive cats. If a cat was
around radioactive material, they would glow, and  then build a folk tradition around it that the
glowing cats are things to avoid and maybe that  persistent story would last over millennia.
It’s an interesting and confounding problem, but  people came up with really creative solutions.
I think it’s evidenced by  what we did when we discovered
different tombs in Egypt and stuff. There’s  no amount of warning that will stop a person
who’s determined to get into a place, even if it  seems intimidating or has traps or whatever it is.
It just makes us more motivated. It’s an  actual problem to think about, for sure.
COWEN: Or you might think there’s  some kind of treasure there, and
they’re trying to scare you  off because it’s valuable.
MARS: Exactly. There’s no way to convey  100 percent what you mean because
places that are protected seem like  there’s something valuable behind it,
and in this case there’s nothing valuable.
COWEN: A related problem: When you’re  coming off the highway, as you well know,
typically you have to go more slowly  on the ramp. If you ought to be going,
say, 40 on the ramp, they’ll tell you ought to  be going 25. Should they just tell us the truth,
or should they systematically lie to us  and say 25, even though 37 might be okay?
MARS: I don’t know. That type of  misinformation—very early on in
my driving career, I learned that 10 miles above  the suggested limit was what they were going for.
COWEN: Usually. Yes.
MARS: I think there’s some utility in me figuring  that out and doing the math as I become a better
driver or a more confident driver or know  the roads better that serves some purpose.
It’s just that that purpose, like  the intention and the effect are
hard to calculate. Would it be better  to tell people the truth? Maybe.
COWEN: Another rule is to double  the number and subtract 10,
if that’s more ambitious in your system.
MARS: There is a lot of driving, at least traffic  devices, and driving in general on the highway in
particular, is all designed around calming your  brain so that you will go that fast because
humans are not evolved to go that fast. If you  were to get out on a highway and stand next to a
sign, most people marvel at the size of a highway  sign. They have no idea that it’s really that big.
Part of that and the dashes in between lanes,  most people estimate when surveyed that a dash
in the dividing line of a highway is two feet  long, when in fact they’re 10 to 15 feet long.
It is all there to calm your  brain at going at high speeds
so that you can go very fast and have it not  freak you out. When you’re going to transition to
tricking people’s brains into going very fast  so that a highway functions, you have to do
things that shock people out of their hypnotic  state to get them into a different driving mode.
An artificially low speed limit or suggested  limit, it makes some sense to do it that way.
Also, as people begin to game it and know what’s  going on, obviously it starts to feel ridiculous.
COWEN: You have a very famous TED Talk on city  flags and what makes for a good city flag.
You’ve propagated the term  “vexillology,” the study of flags.
Why should there be no lettering  on flags? City flags, that is.
MARS: Because a flag is meant to be flying  on a pole, and so it should be seen.
It should effectively work  from backwards and forwards.
It’s just because it has a backside  that you can see, and so it’s not good.
COWEN: What about the other perspective, that  outsiders never see flags? I’ve been, I think,
to the 50 largest American  cities. Often, repeatedly,
there’s not one city flag I could identify  from any one of them until I saw your talk.
MARS: You could identify Chicago  flag if you’ve been to Chicago.
COWEN: No, I couldn’t.
MARS: Really?
COWEN: I absolutely couldn’t.
MARS: Oh, it’s everywhere in  Chicago. That’s interesting.
COWEN: Maybe the purpose of the flag is  to signal to interest groups internally
that they’re respected by the city  or the mayor or the government.
Then you want some lettering.  It looks ugly, but who cares?
MARS: My contention in that talk was, a little  bit, I was just making fun and having fun with
the idea of the design of flags. In general,  what I was discovering as I was thinking
about this was that when cities have good  flags, they use them well and they’re very,
very useful as a municipal device. Chicago is  one of those examples where the Chicago flag is
displayed everywhere and different elements of  it are taken apart and presented. It actually
reinforces and feeds Chicago pride in,  I think, a meaningful and important way.
When you’re in a place that has an  effective flag, usually because it
adheres to these guidelines that Ted Kaye  laid out in his vexillology handbook,
it has this positive reinforcement effect, this  positive feedback loop of having pride in the
city, in displaying a good-looking flag. You  want to display it because it’s good-looking,
it gives you more pride in the place. It  has this nice effect. I think that’s useful
and good. The way to make a good designed  flag is to follow basic principles this way.
If you can love a flag that has lots of colors,  and it’s really busy, and has words on it,
and that gives you the same amount of  pride and has the same amount of utility,
absolutely fine. I’m not there to police  that part of it. I was just giving people
the idea of the tools to make a flag loved because  it is an underused thing in a city to rally around
to give people pride other than sports teams and  other corporate things. This is a thing that we
all own. It’s a piece of design and branding that  is a lovely thing to embrace if it’s beautiful
enough to embrace. That’s the pathway to it is to  make it so that it works in a lot of instances.
Taking words off of it is one of the  things that I think is a good idea. I
think it makes for a cleaner, more beautiful  thing. There’s examples in which—mostly
words I don’t like at all—but there’s examples  in which things that violate flag rules
are, in lovely and amazing ways, that I think  is really beautiful. I think Maryland’s flag
is really beautiful and it harkens back to the  heraldry of Lord Baltimore and Calvert. It’s super
busy and it looks like a racing flag. I think  it’s super gorgeous. You can do it lots of ways.
COWEN: The Brazilian flag, it’s “Ordem  e Progresso,” or “Order and Progress,”
which sometimes is taken almost  satirically, but I quite like it.
MARS: I think the Brazilian flag is great. That’s  another place where they really embrace it. That’s
really it. My goal or my hope for places is just  that recognized flags can be really beautiful.
They’re worth the effort to make them so. They’re  worth lauding and flying. I have a flagpole at
my house. I love putting out flags for various  independence days around the world and various
things that are happening in my life. If I’m going  to visit someplace, I’ll sometimes put a flag up
beforehand. I just think that they’re great  and worth spending some time thinking about.
If it has little words on it, so be it.  The Brazilian flag is an amazing flag.
COWEN: You almost convinced me that  Pocatello, Idaho has the best flag
in the country rather than the worst. I  agree with everything you say about it,
but there’s otherwise no chance you and I  would be mentioning Pocatello, Idaho, right?
MARS: Yes. That’s the thing. I went there to  talk to them about their flag. I called them
out as having the worst flag. The NAVA  survey identified it as the worst flag
in the country. I called them out in this TED  Talk. I was really just having fun with it.
They got in touch. They wanted to redesign the  flag. The truth of the matter is that flag;
it was only official flag in the barest sense.  It was a branding that meant for municipal cars
and things like that, and then they put it on a  flag. They presented it as their official flag,
but it wasn’t made for that. There’s evidence that  it wasn’t made for that because it has a trademark
symbol on it. It has things on it that you  wouldn’t put on a flag, but it was put on a flag.
Then I went to visit them as they were doing  a redesign. I met one of the city leaders.
He was like, “I have to thank you for this because
it would be the worst if we were the  second-worst flag in the country,” then,
“That would be so much worse than being the  absolute worst because then we have motivation
to change, and we had people talking about it, and  it was really fun. The process of figuring out a
new flag was so much fun.” They had a really  good spirit about it. I was very grateful.
They took it really well. I really meant  no harm. It was a fun moment in the talk.
Since that TED Talk has been out, there  have been something in the neighborhood of
250 or 300 municipal flag redesigns in the  country. I think it was just this moment
to just take a look at our place, know that we’re  part of this thing, and make something that we’re
proud of. Even if at the end of it, they go, “You  know what? We love the thing that we had,” that’s
totally fine. I’m happy with it. I like that  people were thinking about it in terms of a city
because I like that as an organizing principle  of people’s lives and their sense of pride.
I love sports, too, like overall sports  teams. Our office was in Oakland downtown
for a long time and our sports teams left.  You can count on Oakland to be Oakland,
but you can’t necessarily count on the A’s being  here or the Warriors playing in the stadium here.
COWEN: How well designed is your  own studio by your own account?
MARS: My own studio?
COWEN: Your own studio.
MARS: I like it. There’s a little closet that  was meant to be a utility closet in my house,
and then they realized that they could put the  water heater somewhere in a crawlspace in another
part of the house, and they had it open. As soon  as I was touring it when I was going to buy it,
I walked in, I was like, “I know exactly  what this room is going to be.” It became
my studio instantly. I have this—it’s called  Cityscape—audio-dampening material that me and my
stepdaughter put up over a couple of days. Then I  actually have still images—that’s the cover of my
book—but it’s done in Softscape, so it dampens  the sound. Yes, I love my studio. It’s great.
I have a standing desk, so I stand all day.
It’s perfectly meant for me. My house is not  the greatest place to put a studio inside of

COWEN: What do you think are the  advantages of doing a podcast or
radio show about visual objects,  but the show itself is audio only?
MARS: I think it has to do with overcoming  people’s biases. If I show you a building, I
think you have a reaction to the building because  of what you’re exposed to and what you like and
don’t like, and for all kinds of reasons, good and  bad. If I could tell you the story of a building,
I can make you fall in love with it. Then you see  it, and then all of a sudden you see the merits,
usually in its function, over your  initial take on its aesthetics.
I think that there’s something about when  I was developing the show 16, 17 years ago,
I was really into that idea of telling the  story of design versus having people react
to the visuals of design, and that it told  a different story that was nice and needed
to be told about intentionality and the things  that we make and do and surround ourselves with.
COWEN: Now, you’ve been extremely productive,  and for a long period of time, in the worlds

MARS: Huh. Unusual?
COWEN: If you said, “Oh, I wake up early  every morning,” not everyone does it,

MARS: Yes. I’m trying to  think. What would be unusual?
When I think about what I am most proud of, I love  being a producer. What I love about it is it means
everything. There’s stages of your job and life  in which you’re cutting tape, or you’re writing
stuff, or you’re reading stuff. There’s times  when you’re trying to solve a problem of what goes
on in the next episode. As my career developed,  I became a producer. My job was to keep a cohort
of people happy and productive, and managing them  in a way where their talents are brought forward.
I loved solving the problem of funding the  show and making sure everyone got paid,

each part of it.” The unusual part is I think  I was very much like a leaf on the wind when it

and thinking of it as a total  problem. No part of it is
